findings.requirement_type: Professional Liability — Minimum Limits Compliance
findings.contract_quote: PROFESSIONAL LIABILITY OR ERRORS AND OMISSIONS LIABILITY: $1,000,000 per claim and aggregate.
findings.policy_quote: $5,000,000 Each Claim / $5,000,000 Aggregate (Dec page MPLDEC 07 19) plus $5,000,000 xs $5,000,000 Convex Excess Tech E&O — $10M total tower.
findings.policy_page: Gemini Dec page; Convex XPL-001 page 6
findings.policy_file: Redacted2025 - 2026 Professional Liability Policy.pdf / RedactedConvex - 2025-2026 Excess Tech EO Policy.pdf
findings.gap_description: Sacramento County requires $1M/$1M minimum Professional Liability with PL expressly excluded from umbrella stacking. Stated tower is $5M primary (Gemini) + $5M excess (Convex) = $10M, materially exceeding the $1M floor. Maricopa does not specify a PL minimum. Convex is a dedicated Excess Professional Liability vehicle, not a commercial umbrella, so the §II.E PL/umbrella prohibition does not apply.
findings.plain_english: On stated limits alone, Run-Test's E&O tower is ten times what Sacramento County requires. The excess layer is properly structured as a dedicated Excess E&O — not a commercial umbrella — so it lawfully sits over the primary E&O.
findings.recommendation: No action required on stated limits. Continue to verify retroactive date and ERP compliance separately (see findings on split limits and retro).

findings.requirement_type: Professional Liability — Split Limits / Tiered Coverage by Wrongful Act Date
findings.contract_quote: $1,000,000 per claim and aggregate. ... If professional liability coverage is written on a Claims Made form: A. The 'Retro Date' must be shown, and must be on or before the date of the Agreement or the beginning of Agreement performance by CONTRACTOR.
findings.policy_quote: Split Limits of Liability (AD 66 16 04 09, End. #4): (a) Wrongful Acts on or after 12/1/2007: $1M each claim / $1M aggregate; (b) Acts on or after 09/06/2019: additional $1M xs $1M; (c) Acts on or after 04/01/2021: additional $3M xs $2M. Effective full $5M/$5M only available for Wrongful Acts first committed on or after 04/01/2021. Wrongful Acts committed between 12/1/2007 and 09/05/2019 are limited to $1M/$1M.
findings.gap_description: Endorsement #4 replaces the policy's stated $5M/$5M limits with a tiered structure pegged to when the underlying Wrongful Act was 'first committed.' Run-Test has 50+ years of operating history and a stated retro of 3/27/2017. A claim alleging a Wrongful Act first committed before 09/06/2019 — even if the claim is reported in the 2025-26 policy year — has only $1M of coverage available from the primary, not $5M. The Convex excess sits over the $5M attachment point, so a Wrongful Act first committed pre-2019 leaves a $4M gap between the $1M primary cap and the $5M Convex attachment that NEITHER policy responds to.
findings.plain_english: On paper you have $10M of E&O. In reality, if a county sues you over something your team did before September 2019, your coverage drops to $1M and there's a $4M dead zone before the excess kicks in. Election operations have long-tail exposure — a ballot processing error from 2018 could surface in a 2026 audit or recount challenge. This is the single biggest hidden gap in the program.
findings.recommendation: Negotiate with Gemini at renewal to: (1) collapse the split-limits endorsement so all covered Wrongful Acts attach to the full $5M tower; or (2) at minimum, advance the Tier (a) cap from $1M to match Tier (c). If carrier refuses, consider repricing with a competing market — multiple Tech E&O carriers will write election-services at unified $5M limits. Also confirm the $4M layer gap (between $1M primary cap and $5M Convex attachment) is communicated to ownership/PE sponsor as a residual exposure.
findings.covered_by_which_policy: Convex Excess only attaches above $5M and follows form, so it inherits the split-limits cap on pre-2019 acts.
discoveryQuestions: Run-Test has been processing ballots for over 50 years. If a county opened a claim today over a ballot or signature-verification issue from your 2017 or 2018 work, do you know how much coverage would actually respond?
Has your prior broker walked you through the difference between the $5M shown on your dec page and the tiered structure inside Endorsement #4?
How comfortable is your PE sponsor with a $4M gap between your $1M limit on pre-2019 acts and where the excess layer attaches?
Are any of your active county contracts based on technology, processes, or relationships that pre-date September 2019?

findings.requirement_type: Professional Liability — Specific Service Retroactive Date Gap (Mail Processing)
findings.contract_quote: The 'Retro Date' must be shown, and must be on or before the date of the Agreement or the beginning of Agreement performance by CONTRACTOR.
findings.policy_quote: Specific Professional Service Retroactive Date (VP 07 84 07 17, End. #1): Retro Date of 04/01/2021 (instead of policy Retro 03/27/2017) applies specifically to 'outbound and inbound mail processing services.'
findings.gap_description: While the master retroactive date is 03/27/2017, Endorsement #1 carves out 'outbound and inbound mail processing services' to a later retro of 04/01/2021. Any mail-processing Wrongful Act first committed between 03/27/2017 and 03/31/2021 is excluded from coverage entirely — a 4-year prior-acts gap on a service line that is core to Run-Test's election mail business.
findings.plain_english: Mail processing — sorting, inserting, and delivering ballot envelopes — is one of your core revenue lines. Coverage for that specific service only goes back to April 2021, even though the rest of your E&O reaches back to March 2017. If a 2018 or 2019 mail-processing error surfaces today (a misdelivered ballot, a wrong address file), the policy won't respond.
findings.recommendation: Push Gemini at renewal to harmonize the mail-processing retro with the master 03/27/2017 retro, or get a written explanation of the underwriting basis (often a prior claim or a service start date). If a hard prior-acts cap is unavoidable, document the date the mail-processing service began to confirm the carve-out doesn't actually exclude any operational period.
discoveryQuestions: When did Run-Test start offering inbound and outbound mail processing as a separate service line — was it before or after April 2021?
Has any prior claim or near-miss involved your mail processing operation that might explain why the carrier carved out a later retro for that service?
If a county discovered a 2019 mail-handling error in a post-election audit, would your operations team know it wasn't covered before the litigation started?

findings.requirement_type: Professional Liability — Client Print Media Exclusion
findings.contract_quote: Coverage shall not contain any provisions which would serve to limit third party action over claims. ... [Insurance must cover] PROFESSIONAL LIABILITY OR ERRORS AND OMISSIONS LIABILITY: $1,000,000 per claim and aggregate.
findings.contract_page: Sacramento §III.E; analogous coverage expectation in Maricopa indemnification §8.1.1
findings.contract_file: Sacramento County and Maricopa County Insurance Requirements
findings.policy_quote: Media Extension Endorsement (AD 66 16 04 09, End. #5), exclusion W.: 'Client Print Media — Claims by clients of the Insured if the Claim is a result of print media or Content furnished by the client.'
findings.gap_description: The Media Extension endorsement adds a 'Client Print Media' exclusion that bars coverage for any client-brought claim arising from print media or Content furnished by that same client. In Run-Test's business model, counties almost universally furnish ballot content, voter data files, candidate lists, and contest layouts — Run-Test prints what the county supplies. If a county sues Run-Test because a printed ballot was wrong (even where the underlying content error originated with the county's data), this exclusion could be triggered to bar coverage.
findings.plain_english: Counties send you the ballot content. You print it. If a county later sues you over a ballot error, the policy contains a clause that says claims by clients arising from content the client itself supplied are excluded. That's nearly every claim scenario in your operating model. This isn't a corner case — it's the front door of your professional liability exposure.
findings.recommendation: URGENT — request that Gemini delete the Client Print Media exclusion (W.) or carve it back so it only applies where the Insured had no role in formatting, processing, or quality-control of the client-furnished content. Document the workflow: counties supply data, but Run-Test's processes (formatting, layout, validation, print integrity, mail merge) are the value-add. Without a carve-back, the bulk of foreseeable claims could be denied. If Gemini will not budge, this becomes a market-replacement conversation at renewal.
discoveryQuestions: Walk me through a typical ballot job — when a county sends you their ballot file, how much of the content is theirs versus what your team formats, validates, or proofs?
Has a county ever come back to you after an election and pointed at something that was wrong on a printed ballot? When that happened, was the source data theirs or yours?

If a county sued you tomorrow over a ballot error, would your team be able to prove the formatting and processing work was your independent professional service rather than just a reproduction of what they supplied?
Did anyone explain Endorsement #5 'Client Print Media' exclusion to you when this policy was bound?

findings.requirement_type: Professional Liability — Delay in Performance/Delivery Exclusion
findings.contract_quote: PROFESSIONAL LIABILITY OR ERRORS AND OMISSIONS LIABILITY: $1,000,000 per claim and aggregate. ... [policies] shall not contain any provisions which would serve to limit third party action over claims.
findings.policy_quote: Amendatory Endorsement — Technology Services Extension (AD 66 16 04 09, End. #6), exclusion D.: '[Excludes] Delay in performance or delivery of Technology Products, Technology Services, or any contractual obligation.'
findings.gap_description: The Tech Services endorsement adds a Delay in Performance exclusion that bars claims arising from delayed delivery of any Technology Product, Technology Service, OR any contractual obligation. Election services run on hard statutory deadlines (ballot mailing windows, Federal Post Card Application deadlines for UOCAVA, certification dates). A delayed ballot mailing causing voter disenfranchisement, a county election deadline miss, or contractual liquidated damages for late delivery are ALL foreseeable claim scenarios — and ALL excluded.
findings.plain_english: Your business runs on statutory deadlines that don't move. If you miss a mailing date or a delivery deadline and a county sues for the resulting harm, your E&O policy says delay claims are excluded. This is the most predictable claim trigger in your industry, and it's specifically excluded.
findings.recommendation: Negotiate carve-back to the Delay exclusion at renewal — at minimum, exclude only delays caused by force majeure or insured-controlled willful misconduct, NOT all delays. Run-Test's underwriter should understand election deadline pressure. Failing carve-back, this is a top-tier replacement priority. In the interim, ensure operations team has bulletproof contractual force-majeure protections AND that any liquidated-damages clauses in county contracts are reviewed by counsel for proportionality.
discoveryQuestions: What's the worst-case scenario if you miss a ballot mailing window for a county on a tight deadline — how would that show up financially?
Have your county contracts ever had liquidated damages or penalty clauses tied to delivery dates? Have any been triggered?
When you priced this E&O policy, was the carrier briefed on the deadline-driven nature of election work?
If a county sued you for damages from a late ballot delivery causing voter disenfranchisement, how would you defend that without policy support for delay claims?

findings.requirement_type: Professional Liability — Notice & Knowledge Officer-Limited Endorsement
findings.contract_quote: RMF General §4 — Notice and Knowledge of Claims: 'Is the policy endorsed so that a covered occurrence is only triggered when the company's officer, the person responsible for insurance, the risk manager, or equivalent is notified — rather than ANY employee's knowledge being imputed to the entity?'
findings.policy_quote: Claim Reporting Provision (AD 66 16 04 09, End. #3): 'Notice trigger limited to awareness by CEO, CFO, General Counsel, or Risk Manager (rather than any Insured). Outside notice still capped at 60 days post-Policy Period.'
findings.gap_description: Endorsement #3 properly limits notice imputation to the four executive functions (CEO, CFO, GC, RM). A line employee's awareness of a potential matter does NOT trigger reporting obligations or void coverage.
findings.plain_english: If a customer-service rep hears about a complaint and doesn't escalate, that won't void your coverage — only awareness at the executive level triggers the reporting clock. This is best-practice language and is correctly in place on the E&O.
findings.recommendation: No action required on this policy. Audit other policies in the program (CGL, Auto, WC, Mgmt Liability, Cyber) for equivalent Notice & Knowledge endorsements; this is a program-level RMF item that should be consistent across all liability policies.

findings.requirement_type: Professional Liability — Hammer Clause (Consent to Settle)
findings.contract_quote: RMF CGL §13 — Duty to Defend / consent-to-settle review.
findings.policy_quote: Consent to Settle Amendment — Miscellaneous (VP 08 51 05 17, End. #16): 'If Insured refuses recommended settlement, carrier liability capped at recommended amount + 80% of subsequent Claim Expenses and Loss. Insured retains 20% of post-refusal costs/loss.'
findings.gap_description: Standard 80/20 hammer clause — if the Insured refuses the carrier's recommended settlement, the Insured bears 20% of every defense dollar and indemnity dollar after the refusal point. Best-in-class hammers are 90/10 or full consent-to-settle (no hammer); 80/20 is mid-market language.
findings.plain_english: If your carrier wants to settle a claim and you don't (because, for example, settlement implies fault on a politically charged election matter), you'll be on the hook for 20% of everything spent after that point — defense costs, judgment, settlement. For a high-value election lawsuit that 20% can be material.
findings.recommendation: At renewal, request 90/10 hammer or full consent-to-settle (no hammer). Election-services claims often have reputational considerations that argue against early settlement — a stronger consent provision protects the insured's strategic interests. If carrier won't move from 80/20, document this as a known constraint in claims-management protocols.
discoveryQuestions: If a county brought a claim that implied election fraud or vote-tampering, would you want the option to fight rather than settle even if the carrier recommended a payment?
Has a prior claim ever put you in a position where the carrier wanted to settle but you wanted to defend on principle?
How would your PE sponsor react if a $2M settlement was recommended but you decided to fight and ended up paying 20% of an even larger judgment?

findings.requirement_type: Professional Liability — Network Security & Privacy Breach Exclusion (cyber risk routed elsewhere)
findings.contract_quote: Cyber, Network Security and Privacy Liability Insurance with a limit of not less than $5,000,000 per occurrence.
findings.policy_quote: Network Security, Privacy Breach and Biometric Identifiers Exclusions (VP 09 97 06 22, End. #21): 'Excludes from Professional Liability any Claim arising from data breach, network security failure, mishandling of confidential/personal information, GLBA, HIPAA, FTC §5(a), DPPA, CA SB 1386 violations.' Biometric statutory violations also excluded.
findings.gap_description: The E&O cleanly carves out cyber/privacy liability so those claims must respond on the standalone Cyber policy. This is intentional architecture (avoids overlap and double-coverage premium), and confirms the program intends Cyber to be the single source of truth for breach exposure.
findings.plain_english: Your E&O policy explicitly says it doesn't cover cyber breaches — that's normal and correct, because you have a standalone Cyber policy for that. The risk is making sure the Cyber policy is actually adequate (see Cyber findings), since this E&O won't backstop it.
findings.recommendation: No action on the E&O. The architectural cleanliness is appropriate. Cyber adequacy must be solved on the AmTrust policy itself.
findings.covered_by_which_policy: AmTrust/Associated Industries Cyber AES1231913 02 (with material limits gaps — see Cyber findings)

findings.requirement_type: Professional Liability — Definition of Professional Services (Election-Specific)
findings.contract_quote: PROFESSIONAL LIABILITY OR ERRORS AND OMISSIONS LIABILITY: $1,000,000 per claim and aggregate.
findings.policy_quote: Professional Services definition (VP 02 75 07 17, End. #9): 'Solely in the performance as an Election Services Firm including but not limited to: Election ballot services, printing ballot services, election printing, petition printing and services, election and petition design, ballot fulfillment, election hardware and software maintenance, support and technical services, outbound and inbound mail processing services, and election & petition products and services.'
findings.gap_description: The Professional Services definition is custom-tailored to Run-Test's actual operations rather than relying on generic 'tech services' or 'consulting' wording. This is the single most important provision on a Professional Liability policy and is correctly drafted.
findings.plain_english: The policy specifically says it covers 'Election Services Firm' work, naming ballot printing, election design, mail processing, hardware/software support — basically what you actually do. This is a strong, well-tailored definition.
findings.recommendation: Maintain at renewal. If any new service lines are added (e.g., voting machine logistics, signature-verification AI, voter outreach analytics), confirm Endorsement #9's enumeration is updated to include them.

findings.requirement_type: Professional Liability — Hardware Malfunction & Electrical Failure Exclusion
findings.contract_quote: PROFESSIONAL LIABILITY OR ERRORS AND OMISSIONS LIABILITY: $1,000,000 per claim and aggregate.
findings.policy_quote: Tech Services Extension (End. #6) exclusions A. & B.: 'Excludes hardware malfunction/defect and electrical failure UNLESS solely caused by Insured's Wrongful Act/negligence.'
findings.gap_description: The carve-back requiring 'solely caused' by Insured's Wrongful Act is unusually narrow. In any concurrent-cause scenario (e.g., a power surge plus an Insured configuration error), the carrier can invoke the exclusion because the Insured cause was not 'sole.' Election technology — printers, scanners, DRE units, ballot-on-demand systems — operates in environments with multiple potential failure causes.
findings.plain_english: If your equipment fails and contributes to a claim, the policy only covers it if your team's action was the SOLE cause. Realistic election-day failures (e.g., heat causes printer jam at the same time a software update is rolled out) involve multiple factors — and that 'solely' word can be used to deny.
findings.recommendation: Push to broaden the carve-back from 'solely' to 'caused in whole or in part' by an Insured Wrongful Act. Standard market language uses concurrent-cause-friendly wording.
discoveryQuestions: How often does election-day equipment failure involve a single root cause versus a combination of environmental, software, and operator factors?
If a printer jams and a software bug both contribute to a delay, would your team be able to definitively say which one 'solely' caused the problem?
Has your incident-response process ever involved root-cause analysis where the answer was genuinely contested?

findings.requirement_type: Professional Liability — Self-Insured Retention Disclosure & County Approval
findings.contract_quote: Any deductibles or self-insured retention that apply to any insurance required by this Agreement must be declared and approved by the COUNTY. (Sacramento §IV) ... County, at its option, may require Contractor to secure payment of such deductibles or self-insured retentions by a surety bond or an irrevocable and unconditional letter of credit. (Maricopa §8.2.6)
findings.contract_page: Sacramento §IV, Page 2 of 4; Maricopa §8.2.6, Page 5 of 41
findings.contract_file: Sacramento County and Maricopa County Insurance Requirements
findings.policy_quote: Self-Insured Retention (VP 06 99 07 17, End. #11): 'Self-Insured Retention of $25,000 per claim. Insured must pay SIR for both Loss and Claim Expenses BEFORE carrier has any obligation. Carrier has no duty to defend until SIR exhausted.'
findings.gap_description: The $25K SIR is meaningful structurally — it's a true SIR (insured retains defense within retention using panel counsel) rather than a deductible. Both Sacramento (§IV) and Maricopa (§8.2.6) require SIRs to be declared and approved; Maricopa reserves the right to require a bond or LOC backing. Need confirmation that (a) all active county contracts have approved this SIR in writing, and (b) no county has yet exercised the bond/LOC option.
findings.plain_english: You have a $25,000 retention before the policy responds. Both Sacramento and Maricopa require you to disclose and get written approval for that retention. We need to confirm that's been done for every active county contract — and that no county has demanded you post a bond or letter of credit to back it.
findings.recommendation: Pull all active county contracts and their COI approvals; confirm the $25K SIR was disclosed and approved in writing for each. If any contract is silent, push the disclosure now to avoid arguing it post-claim. For Maricopa specifically, monitor for any Risk Manager request to bond/LOC the SIR.

findings.requirement_type: Professional Liability — Communicable Disease Exclusion
findings.contract_quote: PROFESSIONAL LIABILITY OR ERRORS AND OMISSIONS LIABILITY: $1,000,000 per claim and aggregate.
findings.policy_quote: Communicable Disease Exclusion (VP 09 68 04 20, End. #20): 'Absolute exclusion for any Claim alleging/arising out of/attributable to any actual or alleged Communicable Disease — including supervisory/hiring/training acts, testing failures, prevention failures, reporting failures, and related communications.'
findings.gap_description: Post-COVID standard exclusion — broad enough to capture any communicable-disease tangential claim (e.g., a poll worker's exposure complaint, a ballot drop-box hygiene allegation, a voter's claim that mail-in processing failed to follow public health protocols).
findings.plain_english: If a future health emergency causes anyone to allege Run-Test failed to properly handle ballots, mailings, or facilities in a disease-safe way, the policy is silent. Low likelihood in normal years, but cannot be eliminated for an election-cycle company that touches public-facing operations.
findings.recommendation: Note as a known program-wide exclusion (industry-standard since 2020). Document in operational protocols that pandemic-related claim scenarios sit on the company's balance sheet. Revisit at renewal if market starts offering carve-backs.
discoveryQuestions: If another public-health emergency landed in the middle of an election cycle, would Run-Test's facility/mail-handling protocols be defensible without insurance backstop?
Have any clients asked questions about Run-Test's pandemic protocols in the last contract cycle?

findings.requirement_type: Professional Liability — Innocent Insured Carve-Back on Criminal Acts Exclusion
findings.contract_quote: RMF Best Practices — innocent insured protection where individual misconduct is alleged.
findings.policy_quote: Amendment Criminal/Dishonest/Knowingly Wrongful Acts (VP 03 08 07 17, End. #12): 'Innocent insured carve-out for natural persons (other than Named Insured) who did not participate in, ratify, or acquiesce. Defense provided until adjudication.'
findings.gap_description: The criminal/dishonest acts exclusion is properly modified with an innocent-insured carve-back — natural-person Insureds who didn't participate in, ratify, or acquiesce in alleged misconduct retain coverage, and defense is provided until final adjudication. Important in an election-services environment where political actors may level fraud allegations against the company without distinguishing among individuals.
findings.plain_english: If somebody at Run-Test was accused of misconduct but a senior executive or director knew nothing about it, the policy still defends the innocent person and the company until a court actually finds them guilty. That's how the language should read.
findings.recommendation: No action. Maintain at renewal.

findings.requirement_type: Professional Liability — Pending and Prior Litigation Date
findings.contract_quote: PROFESSIONAL LIABILITY OR ERRORS AND OMISSIONS LIABILITY: $1,000,000 per claim and aggregate, with retro on or before contract effective date.
findings.policy_quote: Pending and Prior Litigation Exclusion with Date (VP 02 89 10 17, End. #18): 'P&P Litigation Date: 3/26/2017. Excludes Loss/Claim Expenses arising out of pending or prior Claims, suits, or litigation existing prior to 3/26/2017, or future Claims related/associated with such matters.'
findings.gap_description: The P&P litigation date is set at 3/26/2017 — coincident with the master retro. Any pre-2017 latent matter is barred, including future claims that 'relate to' those prior matters. For a 50+ year company, this is a meaningful prior-acts cap and the 'related claims' language is potentially aggressive.
findings.plain_english: The policy excludes anything that was already in litigation or known before March 2017 — and anything that 'relates to' those older matters. The 'relates to' language can be invoked aggressively by carriers to deny new claims that have any thread of connection to old matters.
findings.recommendation: Maintain awareness of any pre-2017 litigation files; ensure they are documented and isolated from current operations to avoid 'related claims' arguments. At renewal, consider whether broader prior-acts language can be negotiated (often tied to a clean disclosure rep on the application).
discoveryQuestions: Were there any pre-2017 county disputes, demand letters, or claims-in-the-making that you'd want to make sure didn't get pulled forward into a 'related claims' argument?
Has your prior carrier or current carrier ever invoked a 'related claims' theory to consolidate or deny coverage?

findings.requirement_type: Professional Liability — Disciplinary Proceeding Sublimit
findings.contract_quote: RMF item — defense sublimits for regulatory/disciplinary actions.
findings.policy_quote: Amended §II.A Disciplinary Proceedings (VP 08 39 05 17, End. #15): 'Disciplinary Proceeding sublimit: $25,000 each / $50,000 aggregate. Deductible does not apply; does not erode Each Claim/Aggregate limits. No duty to appoint counsel.'
findings.gap_description: The Disciplinary Proceeding coverage is sublimited at $25K per proceeding / $50K aggregate, with no carrier duty to appoint counsel. For an election-services firm potentially facing state Secretary of State inquiries, FEC matters, or county audit reviews, $25K of defense will be exhausted quickly by a single competent regulatory defense matter.
findings.plain_english: If a state election authority opens a regulatory inquiry into Run-Test's operations, the policy gives you $25,000 toward defense — that's roughly 60-80 hours of senior outside-counsel time. A serious state inquiry will burn through that in a month.
findings.recommendation: Negotiate higher sublimit at renewal ($100K-$250K is achievable in this market for a clean-loss-history election firm) and ensure carrier accepts duty to defend rather than pay-as-incurred. If carrier holds line, document the gap and ensure D&O / Mgmt Liability or Cyber regulatory-defense coverage is robust.
findings.covered_by_which_policy: Possibly partial — Cyber regulatory defense may apply for cyber-related inquiries; Mgmt Liability may apply for entity regulatory actions. Verify across program.
discoveryQuestions: Have you ever been the subject of a state Secretary of State inquiry, county audit, or other regulatory review of your election operations?
Do you know what your own attorneys would charge for an aggressive multi-state regulatory inquiry — and how that compares to $25,000?

findings.requirement_type: Professional Liability — Subpoena Response Sublimit
findings.contract_quote: RMF item — coverage adequacy for ancillary defense costs.
findings.policy_quote: Subpoena response sublimit: $2,500 per subpoena / $5,000 aggregate (per Dec page Item 4 limits structure).
findings.gap_description: Subpoena response sublimit is materially low ($2,500/$5,000) for a vendor handling 90M+ voter records and frequently subject to election-related discovery in voting-rights, recount, and political litigation involving its county clients.
findings.plain_english: When you get subpoenaed for documents (which is routine for an election vendor), the policy gives you $2,500 per subpoena to pay for legal review and production. That covers maybe a couple of hours of attorney time per subpoena.
findings.recommendation: Negotiate higher subpoena sublimit at renewal — $25K+ per subpoena is reasonable given operational subpoena frequency in election work.
discoveryQuestions: How often does Run-Test get served with subpoenas — for political litigation, recount disputes, voting-rights challenges, or even FOIA-adjacent requests?
How much does it typically cost to respond to a subpoena once your counsel reviews and produces records?

findings.requirement_type: Professional Liability — Carrier Rating Compliance (Sacramento A-VII / Maricopa B++)
findings.contract_quote: Insurance is to be placed with insurers with a current A.M. Best's rating of no less than A-VII. (Sacramento §VI.A.1) ... possessing an AM Best, Inc. category rating of B++. (Maricopa §8.2.1)
findings.contract_page: Sacramento §VI.A.1, Page 3 of 4; Maricopa §8.2.1, Page 5 of 41
findings.contract_file: Sacramento County and Maricopa County Insurance Requirements
findings.policy_quote: Gemini Insurance Company (a Delaware Stock Company; W.R. Berkley group; non-admitted in Arizona — surplus lines).
findings.gap_description: Gemini Insurance Company is a W.R. Berkley subsidiary; W.R. Berkley group is rated A+ XV by AM Best, and Gemini specifically commonly carries A+ ratings. Need to verify the current AM Best rating of Gemini specifically (not just W.R. Berkley) is at A-VII or better at the time each contract was bound and at renewals.
findings.plain_english: Gemini is part of W.R. Berkley — financially a strong group — but contracts measure the specific issuing carrier, not the parent. We need to confirm Gemini's own AM Best rating meets A-VII for Sacramento and B++ for Maricopa, and document it in the COI files.
findings.recommendation: Pull current AM Best rating snapshot for Gemini Insurance Company, document in client file, and flag if a downgrade ever brings it below A-VII for any active CA county contract.

findings.requirement_type: Professional Liability — Surplus Lines / Non-Admitted Carrier (Informational)
findings.contract_quote: ACCEPTABILITY OF INSURERS: Insurance is to be placed with insurers with a current A.M. Best's rating of no less than A-VII. The County Risk Manager may waive or alter this requirement, or accept self-insurance in lieu of any required policy of insurance...
findings.policy_quote: Gemini Insurance Company ... non-admitted in Arizona — surplus lines. Service of process upon John Briggs at 7233 East Butherus Drive, Scottsdale, AZ 85260.
findings.gap_description: Tech E&O is a market routinely placed in the surplus lines / E&S channel — admitted carriers rarely write election-services E&O. AZ guaranty fund does not protect against insolvency of non-admitted carriers (A.R.S. §20-401.01(B)(1)). This is informational, not a critical finding by itself per audit methodology.
findings.plain_english: The carrier isn't licensed in Arizona — it's a surplus lines placement, which is normal and appropriate for tech E&O in the election space. The only consideration is that if the carrier became insolvent, the AZ state guaranty fund wouldn't backstop unpaid claims. Carrier financial strength is therefore the primary protection — see the AM Best verification finding.
findings.recommendation: No action; informational. Maintain AM Best rating verification (see related finding) as the primary carrier-strength protection.

findings.requirement_type: Professional Liability — Claims-Made Form & Retro Date Compliance (Sacramento §V.A and Maricopa §8.2.3)
findings.contract_quote: If professional liability coverage is written on a Claims Made form: A. The 'Retro Date' must be shown, and must be on or before the date of the Agreement or the beginning of Agreement performance by CONTRACTOR. (Sacramento §V.A) ... any retroactive date under the policy shall precede the effective date of this contract... (Maricopa §8.2.3)

findings.requirement_type: Professional Liability — TCPA / Unsolicited Communications Exclusion
findings.contract_quote: PROFESSIONAL LIABILITY OR ERRORS AND OMISSIONS LIABILITY: $1,000,000 per claim and aggregate.
findings.policy_quote: TCPA exclusion (VP 00 06 10 17 §IV.K): 'Excludes claims based on unsolicited faxes and electronic mail.'
findings.gap_description: Standard TCPA exclusion. Run-Test's outbound mail processing for counties is largely transactional and consent-based (voter registration, ballot delivery), but voter outreach mailings, sample ballot pushes, or election notification campaigns could be alleged to fall within TCPA-style consumer protection statutes if a recipient claims lack of consent.
findings.plain_english: TCPA-type lawsuits over unsolicited communications are excluded. Most ballot mail isn't consumer marketing, but if Run-Test ever takes on voter-outreach or election-notification mailings that fall on the wrong side of consent rules, those claims aren't covered.
findings.recommendation: Confirm operationally that Run-Test's mail products are election-mandated communications (ballots, official notices) rather than discretionary outreach. If discretionary outreach is offered, consider standalone media liability or CGL Personal & Advertising Injury coverage adequacy.
findings.covered_by_which_policy: Potentially CGL Personal & Advertising Injury (need GL policy review — not provided in this audit batch).
discoveryQuestions: Does Run-Test handle any voter outreach mailings beyond official ballots and election notices — newsletters, get-out-the-vote campaigns, candidate information?
Have any recipients ever complained that they received election-related mail they didn't ask for?

findings.requirement_type: Excess Tech E&O — Tower Construction & Limits
findings.contract_quote: PROFESSIONAL LIABILITY OR ERRORS AND OMISSIONS LIABILITY: $1,000,000 per claim and aggregate.
findings.policy_quote: Convex Insurance UK Limited XPL000040-0425: $5,000,000 policy limit / $5,000,000 attachment point. Follow form excess to Gemini VIPL056495 primary Tech E&O. Total Tech E&O tower: $10,000,000.
findings.gap_description: Properly structured $5M xs $5M follow-form excess Tech E&O placement creating a $10M total tower. Convex is a dedicated Excess Professional Liability carrier (not a commercial umbrella), which is the correct vehicle to stack on E&O — Sacramento §II.E only prohibits umbrella stacking on PL, not dedicated excess PL.
findings.plain_english: The excess E&O is properly built — $5M sitting over the $5M primary creates a $10M tower for Tech E&O. The structure is appropriate: it's a dedicated Excess E&O policy, not a general umbrella, so the contractual limitation on stacking umbrellas onto E&O doesn't apply.
findings.recommendation: Maintain at renewal. Verify excess attachment point continues to match primary limit (no inadvertent gap if primary limit changes).

findings.requirement_type: Excess Tech E&O — Conditional Follow-Form 'More Restrictive' Clause
findings.contract_quote: UMBRELLA or Excess Liability policies... shall provide liability coverages that at least follow form over the underlying insurance requirements...
findings.policy_quote: Section I (XPL-300): 'If any Underlying Policy includes any more restrictive coverage, terms, definitions, exclusions, conditions, or limitations, then this policy will follow the more restrictive provisions of any Underlying Policy.'
findings.gap_description: Conditional (not pure) follow form. Every restrictive provision on the Gemini primary — split limits, Client Print Media exclusion, Delay exclusion, Hardware/Electrical concurrent-cause language, mail-processing later retro — flows up to and binds the Convex excess. The excess does NOT cure any primary gap; it only amplifies the primary's limits within the primary's scope.
findings.plain_english: The excess policy is only as good as the primary. Every gap in the Gemini primary (the split limits, the Client Print Media exclusion, the Delay exclusion) flows straight up to the Convex excess. Fixing the primary fixes the tower; not fixing the primary leaves a $10M policy with $1M of effective coverage on certain claim types.
findings.recommendation: Treat all primary E&O fixes as urgent — they automatically improve the entire $10M tower. Inversely, any restrictive endorsement added to Gemini at renewal will worsen Convex too, so audit primary endorsements at every renewal cycle.
discoveryQuestions: Do you and your prior broker treat the primary E&O renewal as the more important negotiation, knowing every restriction added there flows up to your $10M total tower?
When the underwriter offers a small premium credit in exchange for a new exclusion on the primary, has anyone walked you through the impact on the excess too?

findings.requirement_type: Excess Tech E&O — Sublimits Not Extended
findings.contract_quote: RMF item — sublimit treatment in excess layers.
findings.policy_quote: Section II (XPL-300): 'If any Underlying Policy grants coverage subject to a sublimit of liability, this policy shall not afford such coverage, however this policy shall recognize any reduction or exhaustion of the Attachment Point by payments with respect to such coverage pursuant to that Underlying Policy.'
findings.gap_description: Any sublimited Gemini coverage (Disciplinary Proceeding $25K/$50K, Subpoena $2.5K/$5K, Supplementary Payments $5K/claim) is NOT extended at the excess layer — but those sublimit payments DO erode the $5M attachment point. Net effect: the insured pays for sublimited coverage with no excess support, but the dollars still consume the path to the excess.
findings.plain_english: If your primary policy has a $25,000 sublimit on a regulatory inquiry, the excess won't add another $25,000 — it just won't respond to that coverage at all. But those $25K of payments DO eat into the $5M you need to use up before excess kicks in. So sublimits on the primary become a one-way street.
findings.recommendation: Negotiate higher sublimits on Gemini primary (see disciplinary proceeding finding). Accept that the excess won't ever supplement sublimits — fix sublimits at the primary level.

findings.requirement_type: Excess Tech E&O — Maintenance of Underlying (Favorable Construction)
findings.contract_quote: RMF Umbrella §6 — Maintenance of underlying insurance.
findings.policy_quote: Section IV.D (XPL-300): If insured fails to maintain underlying or renews/replaces with lesser coverage, Convex is liable only as if the underlying had been fully maintained. Failure to maintain does NOT void the policy but the excess attaches as if the underlying limit were intact (insured eats the gap).
findings.gap_description: This is the favorable of the two common maintenance constructions. The excess is NOT voided for failure to maintain — it simply attaches as if the underlying were fully maintained. Insured assumes the gap dollars but retains the excess capacity above attachment. Compare to the more punitive 'failure-to-maintain-voids-policy' construction common in some commercial umbrellas.
findings.plain_english: If for any reason the primary policy's limits get impaired or replaced with weaker coverage, the excess doesn't disappear — it just acts like the primary was still full strength, and Run-Test eats the gap dollars. That's the better of the two ways this clause can be written.
findings.recommendation: No action — maintain at renewal.

findings.requirement_type: Excess Tech E&O — Right and Duty to Defend on Drop-Down
findings.contract_quote: RMF Umbrella §11 — Right and Duty to defend when underlying limits exhausted.
findings.policy_quote: Section IV.B.2 (XPL-300): 'We will have the right and duty to defend any claim made or suit brought or proceeding instituted against an Insured to which this policy applies if the applicable limits of Underlying Policies have been exhausted.'
findings.policy_page: Not extracted — referenced from analysis JSON
findings.gap_description: Convex grants right AND duty to defend once Gemini exhausts. This is best-in-class for follow-form excess and uncommon in pure-follow-form constructions.
findings.plain_english: Once the primary policy's $5M is paid out, Convex doesn't just write checks — it picks up active defense duty too. That's a strong consumer-friendly provision.
findings.recommendation: Maintain at renewal.

findings.requirement_type: Excess Tech E&O — Underlying Policy Number Discrepancy
findings.contract_quote: Verification of Coverage / COI & Endorsements: 'CONTRACTOR shall furnish the COUNTY with certificates evidencing coverage required below.'

In a coverage dispute, a carrier could (in theory) argue the schedule controls and that Convex sits over a different underlying than the actual primary. findings.requirement_type: Excess Tech E&O — Named Insured Entity Mismatch (LLC vs Inc)
findings.contract_quote: RMF General §3 — Named Insureds list for each policy and flag any missing.
findings.policy_quote: Convex Named Insured: 'Runbeck Election Services, LLC' (LLC). Gemini primary Named Insured: 'Runbeck Election Services, Inc.' (Inc).
findings.policy_file: RedactedConvex - 2025-2026 Excess Tech EO Policy.pdf / Redacted2025 - 2026 Professional Liability Policy.pdf

Convex's Insured definition follows form to the underlying — so if the underlying Insured is 'Inc' but the named Convex insured is 'LLC,' there's at minimum a paperwork mismatch. The Cyber policy was corrected via Policy Change #1 effective 4/1/2025 to reflect 'LLC' — suggesting the LLC is the operative legal entity. This is a no-cost name-change endorsement (typically IL 12 01 11 85 or carrier equivalent). Verify across CGL, Auto, WC, Mgmt Liability, and Umbrella as well — the Cyber cross-reference notes those policies still show 'Inc' too.
discoveryQuestions: What is the operative legal entity for Run-Test today — Runbeck Election Services, Inc. or LLC?
When was the most recent corporate restructuring, and was every insurance policy updated to match?
Are there any subsidiary or affiliate entities that should also be listed (Runbeck Properties, Runbeck Investments, Runbeck Graphics) on every policy in the program?

findings.requirement_type: Cyber — $5M Limit Compliance vs Maricopa Minimum
findings.contract_quote: Cyber, Network Security and Privacy Liability Insurance with a limit of not less than $5,000,000 per occurrence.
findings.policy_quote: Aggregate Limit of Liability: $4,000,000. Defense costs are part of and not in addition to the Aggregate Limit. Aggregate is shared across all 14 coverage lines.
findings.gap_description: Maricopa requires $5M PER OCCURRENCE Cyber. AmTrust policy provides $4M AGGREGATE (not per-occurrence), shared across 14 coverage lines, with defense costs eroding limits. Two separate gaps: (1) $1M+ shortfall on stated limits ($4M < $5M); (2) per-occurrence vs aggregate structure mismatch — aggregate erodes across the year. Effective indemnity capacity on a single significant claim is roughly $800K-$1.6M after defense erosion. This is an uncured contract breach as of policy inception 4/1/2025.
findings.plain_english: Maricopa requires $5M of Cyber. You have $4M, and that $4M is shared across every type of cyber claim and burns down with defense costs. On a single major breach, after lawyers and forensics get paid, your effective coverage is closer to $1M-$1.5M — a fraction of what Maricopa contracted for. You are out of contractual compliance from day one of this policy term.
findings.recommendation: URGENT — increase Cyber tower to at least $5M with structure that satisfies 'per occurrence' language. Options: (1) endorse AmTrust to $5M aggregate (likely additional $5K-$15K premium); (2) add $5M xs $4M excess Cyber layer (cleaner contract compliance and per-occurrence interpretation); (3) replace AmTrust with $5M-limit market (Beazley, AIG, Coalition, At-Bay, etc. routinely write $5M for election-services scale). Recommend Option 2 or 3. Also notify Maricopa Risk Management of cure timeline to mitigate material-breach exposure under §8.2.2 / §8.2.15.
findings.covered_by_which_policy: No Cyber excess in program. Hanover Umbrella (per cross-reference) does NOT follow form to Cyber.
discoveryQuestions: Were you aware that Maricopa requires $5M of Cyber and your current policy provides $4M aggregate with defense inside the limits?
Has your prior broker walked you through what 'shared aggregate across 14 coverage lines' actually means for your claim recovery?

If a major county data event happened in October before the November election, how would you fund the gap between the $4M policy and the actual cost of forensics, breach counsel, regulatory defense, business interruption, and notification at scale?
Has anyone from Maricopa Risk Management ever asked to see the full Cyber policy or just accepted the COI?

findings.requirement_type: Cyber — Defense Within Limits + Shared Aggregate (Effective Capacity Erosion)
findings.contract_quote: Cyber, Network Security and Privacy Liability Insurance with a limit of not less than $5,000,000 per occurrence. The policy shall include, but not be limited to; coverage for... defense, and claims expenses, regulatory defense costs plus fines and penalties...
findings.policy_quote: DEFENSE COSTS ARE PART OF AND NOT IN ADDITION TO THE AGGREGATE LIMIT OF LIABILITY. THE AGGREGATE LIMIT OF LIABILITY AVAILABLE TO PAY LOSS AND THE RETENTION SHALL BE REDUCED AND MAY BE EXHAUSTED BY THE PAYMENT OF DEFENSE COSTS.
findings.gap_description: Defense Within Limits PLUS shared aggregate across 14 coverage lines means a typical cyber event consumes 60-80% of the $4M aggregate on forensics, breach counsel, PR, and regulatory defense before any indemnity is paid. Effective indemnity recovery on a single moderate-to-large event is approximately $800K-$1.6M against a $4M nominal policy. For a vendor handling 90M voter records, this is materially inadequate.
findings.plain_english: Every dollar your lawyers and forensic firm bill on a cyber claim comes out of your $4M policy — and on a real cyber event, the lawyers and forensic firm will eat the majority of that $4M before the first dollar of breach response, regulatory fine, or business interruption indemnity is paid. So your $4M is functionally more like $1M-$1.5M of usable indemnity.
findings.recommendation: Restructure cyber tower with (1) defense-outside-limits or (2) substantially higher limit with stable aggregate, OR (3) layered tower so erosion on the primary doesn't gut total capacity. Coalition, Beazley, AIG and At-Bay routinely offer DOL on $5M+ programs at this revenue band.
discoveryQuestions: Did anyone explain to you that legal fees and forensics on a major cyber claim could consume 60-80% of your $4M before you see a dollar of breach response money?
If a county sued you, regulators investigated, you needed forensics, AND business operations were interrupted — all from one cyber incident — would $4M cover all of that?
Has your IT or security team estimated what a credible breach scenario would cost end-to-end?

findings.requirement_type: Cyber — Cyber Deception / Social Engineering Phantom Coverage
findings.contract_quote: Cyber, Network Security and Privacy Liability Insurance... shall include... computer fraud coverage, funds transfer loss, third-party fidelity, theft, no requirement for arrest and conviction, and loss outside the premises of the named insured.
findings.policy_quote: Cyber Deception/Social Engineering: Limit $250,000 / Retention $250,000.
findings.gap_description: Sublimit equals retention — effective recoverable on any single loss ≤ $250K is $0. On a $300K loss, recovery = $50K. On a $500K loss, recovery = $250K (50% of loss). Maricopa §8.2.13 explicitly requires 'computer fraud coverage' and 'funds transfer loss' which is functionally social engineering / impersonation fraud — the most common large-dollar cyber claim type for vendors managing county AP/AR flows. This is phantom coverage and an uncured contract breach.
findings.plain_english: Social engineering coverage is structured so the retention equals the limit — meaning if a fraudster impersonates a county and tricks your AP team into wiring $200K, you'd recover ZERO. On a $500K loss you'd recover $250K. This is the most common big-dollar cyber claim hitting vendors today, and your coverage on it is essentially worthless.
findings.recommendation: URGENT — increase Cyber Deception limit to at least $1M with retention of $25K-$50K (separate from the $50K policy retention). This is a low-cost endorsement on most cyber forms ($2K-$8K premium typical). Also implement operational controls: callback verification on wire instructions over $25K, dual approval on payment changes, vendor-onboarding identity verification.
findings.covered_by_which_policy: Crime/Fidelity policy may cover — verify if Run-Test maintains a separate Crime policy (not in audit batch).
discoveryQuestions: How often does your AP team process wire transfers or change-of-banking-instructions requests on behalf of county clients or vendors?
If a fraudster spoofed a county elections director's email and instructed your AP team to redirect a $200,000 payment, how would your team detect it?
Did you know that on any single loss up to $250,000, your current cyber policy pays you ZERO under the Cyber Deception coverage?

findings.requirement_type: Cyber — Continuity / Retroactive Date Gap (50+ Year Operating History)
findings.contract_quote: In the event that the insurance required is written on a claims-made basis, Contractor warrants that any retroactive date under the policy shall precede the effective date of this contract...
findings.policy_quote: Continuity Date: 04/01/2023.
findings.gap_description: Continuity Date is 4/1/2023, only 2 years before current inception. Run-Test has 50+ years of operating history with continuous handling of voter data. Persistent threat actors who gained unauthorized access prior to 4/1/2023 — a known threat in the elections sector — would not trigger coverage. Need to confirm against each county contract effective date that the continuity date predates each contract.
findings.plain_english: Your cyber policy only reaches back to April 2023. If a hacker has been quietly inside your systems since 2021 and discovers themselves (or is discovered) tomorrow, the policy may say the breach started before its retro and refuse to respond. For a company your size and tenure, the retro should reach back further.
findings.recommendation: Negotiate retro extension at renewal — 5-7 years is achievable for a clean-claim-history election-services firm. If incumbent carrier won't extend, replace at renewal; most major cyber markets will offer 'full prior acts' or 5+ year retros for this risk profile. Confirm continuity date predates each active county contract effective date.
discoveryQuestions: Has Run-Test been the subject of any prior cyber events — even small ones — that pre-date April 2023?
Does your IT security team monitor for advanced persistent threats that may have established access months or years ago?
When did each of your active county contracts begin? Are any of them effective before April 2023?

findings.requirement_type: Cyber — Additional Insured Status for Maricopa County
findings.contract_quote: The insurance policies required by this contract, except Workers' Compensation and Errors and Omissions, shall name County, its agents, representatives, officers, directors, officials, and employees as additional insureds.
findings.policy_quote: No Additional Insured endorsement visible on Cyber policy. Endorsement schedule (Item 8) blank in extracted excerpt.
findings.gap_description: Maricopa §8.2.7 expressly requires AI status on all policies except WC and E&O. Cyber is NOT carved out and therefore must include AI status. No AI endorsement is visible on the AmTrust Cyber. Many cyber forms do not accommodate AI status; if AmTrust will not endorse, Run-Test is in uncured contract breach and may need to replace cyber to satisfy Maricopa.
findings.plain_english: Maricopa requires the County to be named as an Additional Insured on your Cyber policy. The current policy doesn't appear to do that, and many cyber forms can't be endorsed for AI. You're out of contractual compliance, and curing it may require replacing the cyber carrier.
findings.recommendation: Request AI endorsement from AmTrust immediately for Maricopa County. If AmTrust declines (common in cyber), notify client and (a) shop replacement cyber market that will endorse AI status, OR (b) negotiate written waiver from Maricopa Risk Management acknowledging cyber-form limitations. Don't ignore — Maricopa §8.2.2 makes lapse a material breach.
discoveryQuestions: Did anyone tell you Maricopa requires the County to be named as an Additional Insured on your Cyber policy specifically?
If AmTrust won't endorse the County as AI on Cyber, are you willing to switch carriers, or would you prefer we negotiate a waiver from Maricopa?

findings.requirement_type: Cyber — Waiver of Subrogation for Maricopa
findings.contract_quote: The policies required hereunder, except Workers' Compensation and Errors and Omissions, shall contain a waiver of transfer of rights of recovery (subrogation) against County, its agents, representatives, officers, directors, officials, and employees for any claims arising out of Contractor's work or service.
findings.policy_quote: No Waiver of Subrogation endorsement visible on Cyber policy.
findings.gap_description: Maricopa §8.2.8 requires WoS on all policies except WC and E&O. Cyber is NOT carved out. No WoS endorsement visible on AmTrust Cyber. Uncured contract breach.
findings.plain_english: Maricopa requires your Cyber carrier to waive its right to come after the County for reimbursement after paying a claim. The policy doesn't show that endorsement. If a cyber event involved any County system or action, AmTrust could subrogate against the County — exactly what the contract prohibits.
findings.recommendation: Request WoS endorsement from AmTrust. Most cyber forms accommodate this. If declined, treat as part of the larger replacement conversation alongside the AI gap and the $5M shortfall.
discoveryQuestions: Has your Cyber carrier confirmed in writing that it has waived subrogation rights against Maricopa County?

findings.requirement_type: Cyber — Primary & Noncontributory for Maricopa
findings.contract_quote: Contractor's insurance shall be primary insurance as respects County, and any insurance or self-insurance maintained by County shall not contribute to it.
findings.policy_quote: No Primary & Noncontributory endorsement visible on Cyber policy.
findings.gap_description: Maricopa §8.2.4 program-level P&NC requirement applies to all required policies including Cyber. No endorsement visible.
findings.plain_english: Maricopa requires your insurance to pay first before any County coverage gets touched. The Cyber policy doesn't have that endorsement. Lower-priority gap than AI/WoS but still a contract breach.
findings.recommendation: Request P&NC endorsement on Cyber from AmTrust at next opportunity (often automatic on AI endorsement; verify language).
discoveryQuestions: Does your Cyber COI to Maricopa indicate primary and noncontributory status?

findings.requirement_type: Cyber — Designated Entity 30-Day Cancellation Notice
findings.contract_quote: Applicable to all insurance policies required within the insurance requirements of this contract, Contractor's insurance shall not be permitted to expire, be suspended, be canceled, or be materially changed for any reason without 30 days prior written notice to Maricopa County.
findings.policy_quote: No Designated Entity Notice of Cancellation endorsement visible. Endorsement schedule blank in extracted excerpt.
findings.gap_description: Maricopa §8.2.15 requires direct 30-day cancellation/material-change notice to the County, not the standard ACORD COI disclaimer. Cyber forms don't always include this; need to confirm or endorse. Note: Sacramento §VI.A.2 places notification obligation on the Contractor (not the carrier), so a Designated Entity NOC isn't required there — but Maricopa is more demanding.
findings.plain_english: Maricopa requires your Cyber carrier to give the County 30 days' written notice if anything material changes on the policy or the policy gets cancelled. The standard ACORD COI 'endeavor to notify' language doesn't satisfy this — you need an actual endorsement. If it's not on the policy, you're in breach of §8.2.15.
findings.recommendation: Request Designated Entity NOC endorsement on Cyber for Maricopa County (and any other counties with similar requirements). Verify across all required policies in the program (CGL, Auto, WC, Umbrella, Mgmt Liability — all currently listed in cross-reference but not in this audit batch).
discoveryQuestions: Has the carrier provided a Designated Entity Notice of Cancellation endorsement naming Maricopa County?
If the Cyber policy were cancelled mid-term, would Maricopa get 30 days' written notice directly from the carrier?

findings.requirement_type: Cyber — Proof of Loss Sublimit
findings.contract_quote: Cyber, Network Security and Privacy Liability Insurance with a limit of not less than $5,000,000 per occurrence. The policy shall include... defense, and claims expenses...
findings.policy_quote: Proof of Loss sublimit: $250,000 / Retention $50,000.
findings.gap_description: Proof of Loss sublimit caps forensic accounting expense at $200K (after $50K retention). For a multi-million-dollar BI claim documentation, $200K of forensic accounting may be inadequate, particularly given that the policy's $4M shared aggregate makes BI claim proof-up the most likely scenario where forensic accounting is needed.
findings.plain_english: Proving up a business-interruption loss requires a forensic accountant and that work is sublimited to $200K. On a serious BI claim that work alone can run $300K-$500K. You'd be funding the gap.
findings.recommendation: Negotiate higher Proof of Loss sublimit at renewal — $500K is achievable in most market.
discoveryQuestions: If you had to prove a $3M business-interruption loss to the carrier, how much would your CFO need in forensic-accounting fees to do that?

findings.requirement_type: Cyber — Choice of Law (NY for AZ Insured)
findings.contract_quote: Compliance with insurance requirements... and applicable state law.
findings.policy_quote: Choice of Law: New York.
findings.gap_description: Insured is Arizona-domiciled with operations in 31+ states. NY choice-of-law clause affects litigation venue, recoverable damages categories, punitive damage availability, and statute-of-limitations interpretation in any coverage dispute. Not a coverage gap per se but a structural item to flag.
findings.plain_english: If you ever fight your cyber carrier over coverage, the dispute will be decided under New York law, not Arizona's. Different states interpret policy language differently — NY is generally insurer-friendly on choice-of-law issues. Worth knowing, not necessarily worth changing.
findings.recommendation: No immediate action. Review at renewal whether replacement market offers AZ choice-of-law (some carriers will). Ensure outside counsel familiar with NY coverage law is identified for any future cyber dispute.

findings.requirement_type: Cyber — Surplus Lines Carrier (Informational)
findings.contract_quote: ACCEPTABILITY OF INSURERS: Insurance is to be placed with insurers with a current A.M. Best's rating of no less than A-VII... (Sacramento §VI.A.1) ... AM Best, Inc. category rating of B++ (Maricopa §8.2.1)
findings.contract_file: Sacramento County and Maricopa County Insurance Requirements

findings.requirement_type: Maricopa — Indemnification Comparative-Negligence Compatibility
findings.contract_quote: To the fullest extent permitted by law, and to the extent that claims, damages, losses, or expenses are not covered and paid by insurance purchased by the contractor, the contractor shall defend, indemnify, and hold harmless the County (as Owner)... but only to the extent caused by the negligent acts or omissions of the contractor, a subcontractor, anyone directly or indirectly employed by them, or anyone for whose acts they may be liable... The scope of this indemnification does not extend to the sole negligence of County.
findings.policy_quote: Indemnification scope is limited to extent of contractor negligence; AZ comparative negligence applies; sole-negligence carve-out for County.
findings.gap_description: Maricopa's indemnification clause is properly drafted under AZ A.R.S. §32-1159 and §34-226 — limited to extent of contractor negligence rather than unlimited or 'sole negligence' tied. Insurable contractual liability under standard CGL contractual liability coverage. No special endorsement required.
findings.plain_english: Maricopa's indemnification language is reasonably balanced — you're only on the hook to the extent your team (or subs) was negligent. Arizona's comparative-fault rules apply. This is the kind of clause your standard CGL contractual liability coverage handles, assuming the CGL has blanket contractual.
findings.recommendation: No action on contract scope. Verify CGL has blanket contractual liability (standard ISO CG 00 01 includes via the 'insured contract' definition) when CGL is audited.

findings.requirement_type: Sacramento — COI & Endorsement Copies Required Pre-Performance
findings.contract_quote: CONTRACTOR shall furnish the COUNTY with certificates evidencing coverage required below. Copies of required endorsements must be attached to provided certificates. ... All certificates, evidences of self-insurance, and additional insured endorsements are to be received and approved by the County before performance commences.
findings.policy_quote: Endorsement copies (not just COI references) must be attached and approved by County before performance.
findings.gap_description: Sacramento requires actual endorsement COPIES — not just COI references — to be attached and approved before performance commences. County also reserves right to require certified copies of policies. Process verification needed: confirm Run-Test's COI delivery to Sacramento includes copies of AI, WoS, P&NC, and Designated Entity NOC endorsements (where required), not just ACORD COI line items.
findings.plain_english: Sacramento doesn't accept just an ACORD certificate — they want actual copies of the endorsements showing them as Additional Insured, Waiver of Subrogation, etc. We need to confirm that whoever issued COIs to Sacramento attached the actual endorsement forms.
findings.recommendation: Pull Run-Test's most recent Sacramento County COI submissions and confirm endorsement copies were attached. Implement a checklist for Sacramento and similar high-bar counties (Maricopa) to ensure full endorsement packages travel with COIs going forward.

findings.requirement_type: Both Counties — 30-Day Claim Notice / 10-Day Lawsuit Notice Obligation
findings.contract_quote: If any claim for damages is filed with CONTRACTOR or if any lawsuit is instituted against CONTRACTOR, that arise out of or are in any way connected with CONTRACTOR's performance under this Agreement and that in any way, directly or indirectly, contingently or otherwise, affect or might reasonably affect COUNTY, CONTRACTOR shall give prompt and timely notice thereof to COUNTY. Notice shall be prompt and timely if given within thirty (30) days following the date of receipt of a claim or ten (10) days following the date of service of process of a lawsuit.
findings.policy_quote: Contractor's contractual notice duty to County: 30 days from claim receipt; 10 days from service of process. Independent of carrier notice obligations.
findings.gap_description: This is a Run-Test operational obligation, not an insurance endorsement. Need to verify that Run-Test's claims-management protocol includes this 30/10-day pass-through to county clients. Failing to notify within window is a contract breach independent of insurance coverage.
findings.plain_english: Sacramento expects to hear about any claim related to Run-Test's work for them within 30 days (or within 10 days of being served with a lawsuit). This isn't an insurance issue — it's an operational notification process. We need to make sure your claims-management workflow has Sacramento and any other county on the notification routing.
findings.recommendation: Document and implement a claims-incident protocol that includes county client notification within contractual timeframes. Maintain a list of every active county/government client and the specific notification address per contract. Review at each contract renewal.
discoveryQuestions: When you've received claims or lawsuits in the past, how did you handle notifying the affected county clients?
Is there a written incident-response protocol that maps each county's notification requirements?

findings.requirement_type: Cyber — Biometric Identifiers Coverage (BIPA-Style)
findings.contract_quote: [Cyber] policy shall include... invasion of privacy (regardless of the type of media involved in the loss of private information)...
findings.policy_quote: E&O End. #21 (VP 09 97 06 22) excludes biometric identifier statutory violations from E&O. Cyber policy biometric coverage scope not visible in extracted excerpt.
findings.gap_description: If Run-Test handles signature data, voiceprint authentication, fingerprint or other biometric data in any election authentication or voter-verification process, Biometric Information Privacy Act (BIPA-style) statutes in Illinois, Texas, Washington, and other states create regulatory and class-action exposure. E&O excludes biometric statutory claims; Cyber must cover or this is a true uninsured exposure.
findings.plain_english: If Run-Test ever processes signatures, voice prints, fingerprints, or any other biometric data — even just signature-verification on mail ballots — there are state laws (Illinois BIPA most famously) that create automatic statutory damages and class-action exposure. Your E&O specifically excludes this. We need to verify your Cyber policy actually covers it.
findings.recommendation: Pull full Cyber policy form. Specifically verify whether biometric statutory violations (BIPA, Texas CUBI, WA HB 1493, etc.) are covered, sublimited, or excluded. If excluded, this is a genuine coverage gap that needs resolution before any biometric-touching service line expands.
discoveryQuestions: Does Run-Test's signature-verification process for mail ballots involve any storage or processing of signature data?
Are you offering any biometric authentication services (fingerprint, voiceprint) to counties?
Have you operated in Illinois, Texas, or Washington — states with active biometric privacy statutes?
